subject: English
summaryPoints: Conditional sentences span four types: Type 0 (universal/scientific truths: simple present in both clauses), Type 1 (probable future: simple present in if-clause, will/can + V1 in main clause), Type 2 (unreal/hypothetical present: simple past/were in if-clause, would/could + V1 in main clause), and Type 3 (counterfactual past: past perfect in if-clause, would/could/might + have + V3 in main clause).
In conditional Type 2 and expressions of hypothetical wishes, the subjunctive form 'were' is universally applied to all grammatical persons (including 'If I were', 'If he were').

Direct speech shifts to reported speech via backshifting tenses when the reporting verb is in the past (simple present -> simple past, present continuous -> past continuous, present perfect/simple past -> past perfect), alongside necessary deictic pronoun, time, and position transformations.

Time and place deictic shifts in reported speech convert 'now' to 'then', 'today' to 'that day', 'yesterday' to 'the day before/the previous day', 'tomorrow' to 'the next/following day', 'ago' to 'before', and 'here' to 'there'.

Separable phrasal verbs allow noun objects to appear either after the particle or between the verb and particle, whereas pronoun objects must strictly appear in the mid-position between the verb and particle (e.g., 'wrote them down', NOT 'wrote down them').

Argumentative writing relies on establishing a clear premise, organizing body paragraphs around corroborating evidence, refuting counterarguments, and utilizing transitional markers for adding points, stating opinions, and comparing conflicting views.

formulas.label: Complete Conditional Type 2 Formula
formulas.expr: If + Subject + Simple Past (V2 / were) + , + Subject + would/could/might + V1(base)

formulas.label: Complete Conditional Type 3 Formula
formulas.expr: If + Subject + had + V3(past participle) + , + Subject + would/could/might + have + V3(past participle)

formulas.label: Reported Speech Tense Backshift
formulas.expr: V1/do/does -> V2/did  |  is/am/are -> was/were  |  has/have + V3 -> had + V3  |  V2/did -> had + V3  |  will/can -> would/could

formulas.label: Phrasal Verb Pronoun Object Syntax Rule
formulas.expr: Verb + Pronoun (it/them/him/her/us/me) + Particle  (Never: Verb + Particle + Pronoun)

examTip: A major trap in EUEE reported speech is forgetting to convert simple past (V2) in direct speech into past perfect (had + V3) in indirect speech. Also, with separable phrasal verbs, pronoun objects must always go between the verb and the preposition: 'He picked it up' is correct; 'He picked up it' is strictly incorrect.

keyDefinitions.definition: A complex sentence consisting of a subordinate condition clause (protasis) and a principal result clause (apodosis) expressing hypothetical, probable, or impossible outcomes.
A syntactic transformation recounting what someone stated without quoting their exact words verbatim, requiring tense backshifting and deictic adjustments.
Linguistic features specifying time, place, and person that shift relative to the speaker's spatial and temporal perspective when reported.
A transitive phrasal verb whose particle can be separated from the verb by an intervening nominal or pronominal direct object.
